transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-01
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Natarajan (Redwood SE), Evan Cruz (Halcyon, VP Eng), Maya Singh (Halcyon, SRE), Oliver Park (Halcyon, CTO)

Auto-summary: Discussed multi-region routing, automatic fallback policies (model variant and regional fallback), SLA expectations for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, and security/compliance needs (KMS, audit logs, SSO). Decided to run a pilot and schedule a deeper technical session.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everybody thanks for joining, i'm Jordan from Redwood, we've got Priya from our infra / se team.. thanks for making time
[00:12] Evan: yeah thanks Jordan, appreciate it. quick context — we're evaluating options for embedding/assistant features for our B2B product, super latency sensitive, like p95 under 400ms for short prompts — so reliability is huge
[00:25] Priya: got it — and today we'd like to focus on incident tolerance, multi-region fallbacks, and what you can expect from Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private in terms of SLOs and controls
[00:34] Oliver: right, and we have a pretty strict on-call policy so if a model endpoint flaps it can mean support pages degraded — that's bad for us
[00:42] Maya: and we also have data residency constraints for some customers in europe, so any multi-region routing has to preserve residency for sensitive workloads
[00:50] Jordan: makes sense. quick high level: Hosted gives you fastest time to value and we have regional routing + automated fallback; Dedicated gives reserved GPU capacity + SLA backed latency and uptime; Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you full control over network and keys. but let's get into fallbacks — we do layered fallbacks: first route to a healthy replica in-region, then cross-region, then model-variant fallback (smaller or quantized model) to maintain availability.
[01:25] Evan: when you say model-variant fallback, is that automatic or something we'd configure? and how do you avoid quality regressions when falling back?
[01:34] Priya: good q — we let customers define policies. you can set route order + acceptable latency thresholds + model families. we also attach regression monitors to the rollout — quick eval sets that run on fallback traffic so you can surface quality regressions. sometimes it's manual (A/B canary) but you can enable automatic fallback if it meets your risk tolerance
[02:15] Maya: what about prefix cache / kv cache behavior across failovers? like if we hit an out-of-region replica does it lose the cache and spike latencies?
[02:25] Priya: yes there is a tradeoff — our KV cache is per-replica. when you fail to a new region you will not have hot prefix cache for those sessions, so you'll see a cold-start token cost on first few requests. we do proactive warming strategies for high-critical paths and also keep a shared read-through cache for embeddings in some setups. the net effect is a few hundred milliseconds on first request but subsequent calls warm quickly
[03:05] Oliver: that might be okay if it's rare, but our SLO needs that 95th to be stable. what do SLAs look like for Dedicated vs Hosted?
[03:15] Jordan: Hosted SLA for enterprise tier is 99.9% regional availability with best-effort latency targets; Dedicated has contractual SLOs for throughput and tail latency with credits for misses. Private is customer-managed so Redwood provides support SLAs but you control infra. we can share the SLA doc after the call
[04:00] Evan: and multi-region, do you do active-active or active-passive routing? we prefer active-active for faster failover
[04:08] Priya: we support both. active-active is our recommended pattern for latency-sensitive global apps — traffic is routed by region preference but can fail-over to the nearest healthy region. active-passive is simpler to reason about but longer failover time.
[04:40] Maya: is cross-region traffic encrypted end to end? and how do you handle keys — we need HSM/KMS integration and we can't have plaintext tokens leaving our VPC for Private deployments
[04:52] Jordan: yes encryption in transit is standard TLS. for Hosted we integrate with customer-managed KMS via bring-your-own-key for enterprise — keys never leave the KMS, and for Dedicated we can bring the HSM/KMS into the deployment. for Private on-prem, you manage keys entirely. we'll attach the security whitepaper — see link (note: placeholder) https://redwood.example/security-pack.pdf
[05:30] Oliver: what's the expected impact on cost if we configure aggressive fallbacks to smaller models? we don't want to blow up cost on a failover event
[05:38] Priya: smaller models reduce compute cost per-token but you also pay for extra routing; fallback frequency is the key driver. we provide cost-aware policies where you can set a budget cap; if failovers exceed budget you can switch to a cheaper routing (e.g., degrade to non-streaming or increase batching). Redwood Optimize can give recommendations for quantization and batching to hit cost targets
[06:20] Evan: can you do region-level throttles or quotas so we don't overload another region in a failover?
[06:27] Priya: yes you can set per-region quotas and we have circuit-breakers to stop cascading failures. we also do gradual rollouts and traffic shaping during recovery window
[07:00] Jordan: quick note — we also keep request tracing and per-route dashboards in Console so your SREs can track failovers and the fallback chain; you'll see model pick, region, latency, and error codes
[07:15] Maya: that dashboard access is critical for us — we need audit logs for compliance as well
[07:20] Jordan: yep audit logs + request-level traces and token-level cost breakdown are available; we can push logs to your SIEM or to S3.
[08:30] Evan: ok deeper technical: Priya can you sketch how a typical failure path looks end-to-end? like request comes in, region unhealthy, route selection, model variant fallback, and finally client response — want to understand timing and potential cold cache penalties
[08:46] Priya: sure — step 1: request lands on edge gateway, edge consults routing policy and health checks. if regional capacity is healthy, route to in-region pool. if health fails or latency thresholds breached, gateway evaluates fallback rules: same-region replica first, if unavailable route to remote region X, if still failing evaluate model-variant fallback — that can be a smaller quantized model (e.g., 4-bit quant) which has faster warmup. at each hop we log reason codes. timing: cross-region reroute adds network RTT; model-variant fallback adds model load time and cold KV cache penalty. overall failover to remote region + smaller model roughly 200-600ms depending on sequences and cache state
[10:00] Oliver: is there a way to maintain sticky sessions or preserve KV cache across regions?
[10:07] Priya: not currently at per-session level across regions for real-time inference; we recommend state replication for embeddings or use a shared fast read-through cache in a single region with geo-replication for embeddings only. session stickiness is possible at the edge if you prefer it — but it reduces ability to failover to other regions automatically
[11:00] Maya: about observability — do you keep raw request/response bodies for retros? we have strict PII rules so we'd rather only have hashed traces
[11:10] Jordan: you control retention and PII stripping. for Hosted we can redact or hash payloads before storing traces; Dedicated you can choose storage location; Private you control everything.
[12:00] Evan: ok, legal and procurement will ask about data residency and audit logs — can you provide SOC2 + ISO docs and a network diagram for Dedicated?
[12:10] Jordan: yes, sending security pack now is on my list. will include SOC2, ISO, network diagrams, and our standard encryption and key flow diagrams.
[12:30] Priya: another note on canaries — we do canary rollouts by model version and route, you can set traffic % increments and automatic rollback on error rate or quality regression thresholds
[13:15] Oliver: good. what about scaling behavior under bursty workloads — we see traffic spikes from product launches, tens of thousands of concurrent chats; do you do autoscaling warm pools?
[13:26] Priya: Dedicated has warm pools and optional pre-warming. we support autoscaling with a configurable scale-back cooldown and burst buckets; for Hosted we auto-scale but the tail can be higher during abrupt surges which is why Dedicated is recommended for massive, predictable spikes
[14:00] Evan: any customers with a similar profile you can point to? financial/saas with global users?
[14:07] Jordan: yes, we have customers in fintech and retail that run active-active multi-region setups — i'll share anonymized references and a benchmark doc
[15:00] Maya: benchmark — we'd like to run a pilot that simulates our traffic profile, measure p50/p95/p99 and observe failover behavior. can Redwood provision an environment for that?
[15:10] Priya: yes, we can provision a pilot environment on Dedicated or Hosted with reserved capacity for 2 weeks. we'll instrument the scenarios and share metrics.
[16:00] Evan: what level of control do we have over model versions and package updates? we can't have surprise model changes mid-quarter
[16:08] Priya: you can pin model versions and control rollouts. by default Redwood publishes patch release notes but we won't change your pinned model without your sign-off.
[17:00] Jordan: quick objection we often hear — "Hosted is cheaper but not reliable enough" — many customers mitigate by using regional redundancy and fallback policies; Dedicated is for teams that need contractual SLOs.
[17:20] Oliver: cost-wise if we do Dedicated reserved but need more throughput occasionally, do you have burst capacity?
[17:28] Jordan: yes Dedicated supports burst pools for short windows. pricing sheet will show commit tiers + overage burst rates.
[18:00] Maya: about private deployments — if we go Private on-prem there's a support model? we can't manage everything ourselves during an incident
[18:08] Priya: Redwood offers enterprise support + runbooks for Private with optional managed services add-on where we operate parts of the control plane. in that scenario we still keep keys in your KMS if required
[19:00] Evan: on routing policies can we prefer region for some customers (residency) but allow others global routing?
[19:08] Priya: yes routing policies are per-tenant or per-route. you can pin a customer to eu-only or allow global failover for others.
[20:00] Oliver: how long does it take to provision Dedicated capacity?
[20:07] Jordan: depends on region and commit, but typical lead time is 2-6 weeks for initial pools; Private on-prem is longer (varies by hardware procurement)
[21:00] Maya: any recommendations to reduce cold-start during failover?
[21:08] Priya: warm pools, proactive prefix warming, and smaller model caches help. also for chat history we suggest KV prefetch heuristics on failover windows
[22:00] Evan: any gotchas with autoscaling and stateful KV caches?
[22:08] Priya: you have to consider cache affinity and eviction during scale-in; we provide eviction-safe policies but it requires some tuning
[24:00] Jordan: quick recap — Halcyon needs: 1) pilot to validate p95/p99 and failover; 2) security docs for procurement; 3) technical deep dive with Maya and infra team; 4) pricing for Dedicated w/ burst.
[24:22] Evan: yes that covers it
[25:00] Maya: i'll add that we want clear audit logs for every failover event, including reason codes and affected sessions
[25:10] Priya: agreed, we log reason codes, model variant, region, and concisely store traces; retention configurable
[27:00] Oliver: if we detect a regression after a fallback (quality drop), can we auto-route back to original model once healthy, or is that manual?
[27:12] Priya: you can configure automatic rollback when a model's quality metric recovers, or you can make it manual — both supported
[28:00] Evan: timeline-wise — procurement expects a vendor evaluation within two weeks; we'd like to start pilot asap
[28:08] Jordan: we can start pilot next week; Priya will share benchmark template and requirements today
[30:00] Maya: curious — how do you handle dependency on cloud provider region outages? if a whole cloud region is down, do you have multi-cloud options?
[30:12] Priya: yes, our multi-region fabric can be multi-cloud; we can route to another cloud provider/region if configured. that said, cross-cloud adds complexity for data residency and networking, but it's supported for critical workloads
[32:00] Evan: any rate limiting best practices for client SDKs? we want to avoid retry storms on failover
[32:10] Jordan: client-side exponential backoff plus jitter and bounded retries; server side we provide quotas and token bucket shaping. also use streaming vs batch appropriately
[33:00] Oliver: can we get a troubleshooting playbook for typical incident types? e.g., model OOM, node failover, cross-region network blip
[33:10] Priya: yes, we'll share an incident playbook with runbooks for each error class and suggested mitigations and alert thresholds
[34:30] Evan: ok pricing question again — if fallback hits more expensive cross-region instances, do you bill at the region the compute runs in?
[34:40] Jordan: billing is per-execution location and model type; cross-region compute is billed at the region where it ran. we include cost-awareness tooling so you can set budget caps and alerts
[36:00] Maya: one more — can Redwood provide metrics downsampled for SRE dashboards so we don't store everything at full fidelity?
[36:08] Priya: yes we can stream metrics to your monitoring and support configurable granularity and retention
[38:00] Evan: let's talk pilot scope — our requirements: 1) simulate 10k concurrent chats, 2) test failover by simulating region outage, 3) measure p50/p95/p99, 4) check KV cache cold start behavior
[38:18] Priya: noted. we'll include warm/cold scenarios and model-variant fallback frequency tests.
[40:00] Jordan: next steps recap: I'll send security pack & SLA PDFs; Priya will send benchmark plan and pilot provisioning checklist; Halcyon to confirm pilot endpoints and timeline; schedule tech deep dive early next week
[41:10] Evan: sounds good. who should I route procurement questions to?
[41:15] Jordan: route procurement to me and cc our legal contact — i'll include contract template in the security pack
[42:00] Maya: thanks — a small nit: any chance you can include an example of the exact log entry we get for a failed health-check? it's easier for us to plug into alert rules
[42:10] Priya: yes we'll add sample log snippets in the playbook
[44:00] Oliver: any concerns about long-term cost predictability with heavy fallback usage?
[44:08] Jordan: it's predictable if you set budgets and use Optimize recommendations; uncontrolled fallbacks can increase spend, but that's exactly why we have tooling + alerts
[46:00] Evan: last question — do you support zero-downtime model rollbacks if a new model causes regressions?
[46:08] Priya: yes canary then immediate rollback on metrics; zero-downtime for the vast majority of cases as long as you maintain a warm pool of prior model variant
[48:00] Maya: okay, anything else from Redwood?
[48:05] Jordan: no, just to say we'll follow up with docs + benchmark plan and get the pilot scheduled.
[49:00] Evan: thanks everyone.
[50:00] Oliver: thanks, bye
[54:00] End of call
